top5.diagnosis: Granulomatous tubulointerstitial nephritis with hypercalcemia (likely sarcoidosis or drug-induced, e.g., quetiapine/ranitidine) plus monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (IgM kappa)
top5.rationale: Chronic active tubulointerstitial nephritis with noncaseating granulomas and hypercalcemia suggests granulomatous interstitial nephritis; coexisting IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy may be incidental but could contribute via light-chain tubulopathy.

top5.diagnosis: Multiple myeloma (kappa light-chain) with cast nephropathy and hypercalcemia
top5.rationale: Bone marrow shows 7% monoclonal kappa plasma cells, serum/urine kappa light chains, osteopenia and lucent bone lesions; hypercalcemia and renal failure fit myeloma, though renal biopsy lacks cast nephropathy.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (renal and/or disseminated) with granulomatous interstitial nephritis and hypercalcemia
top5.rationale: Positive tuberculin skin test, immigrant from Europe/South America, granulomatous nephritis, and hypercalcemia due to granulomatous vitamin D activation; urine cultures negative but extrapulmonary TB can be paucibacillary.

top5.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis with renal granulomatous interstitial nephritis and hypercalcemia
top5.rationale: Noncaseating granulomas in kidney, hypercalcemia, mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy (though calcified and FDG-avid), and elevated ACE? (not reported) fit sarcoidosis; renal failure from granulomatous interstitial nephritis.

top5.diagnosis: Waldenström's macroglobulinemia / IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy with hypercalcemia and renal involvement
top5.rationale: IgM kappa M component, elevated IgM, kappa Bence Jones proteinuria, and marrow plasmacytosis suggest IgM gammopathy; hypercalcemia and renal failure can occur via light-chain deposition or hyperviscosity, though less typical.
High-risk HPV exposure (condylomas), AIDS history, and persistent rectal pain/blood unresponsive to antimicrobials with negative infectious workup strongly suggest malignancy requiring biopsy.
Severe immunosuppression history (CD4 nadir 6) predisposes to CMV tissue-invasive disease which can present as proctitis with bloody discharge despite current viral suppression.
History of rectal HSV and condylomas; mucosal shedding or deep ulceration may be missed by superficial swabs, necessitating PCR or biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

Unprotected receptive anal intercourse is a major risk factor; LGV causes severe proctocolitis that mimics IBD or cancer and requires specific nucleic acid testing not always included in standard panels.

Family history of Crohn's and presentation of chronic rectal pain/discharge could represent new-onset inflammatory bowel disease, though less likely than infectious/malignant etiologies in this demographic.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (reactivation, disseminated) with renal and pulmonary involvement
top5.rationale: Positive tuberculin skin test, prior negative evaluation, immigration from Europe/South America, construction work exposure, granulomatous tubulointerstitial nephritis, and hypercalcemia from granulomatous disease all fit reactivated TB.

top5.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis with renal granulomatous interstitial nephritis and hypercalcemia
top5.rationale: Granulomatous nephritis, hypercalcemia, mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy with FDG avidity, and elevated ACE (though normal here) fit sarcoid, but calcified nodes and positive PPD make TB more likely.

top5.diagnosis: IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) with light-chain tubulointerstitial nephritis
top5.rationale: IgM kappa M component, elevated free kappa light chains, kappa Bence Jones proteinuria, and renal biopsy showing plasma cells and histiocytes suggest a plasma-cell dyscrasia causing renal injury.

top5.diagnosis: Multiple myeloma (smoldering or active) with hypercalcemia and renal failure
top5.rationale: Hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, lytic bone lesions on skeletal survey, 7% plasma cells with monoclonal kappa, and M component all meet CRAB criteria.

top5.diagnosis: Histoplasmosis (disseminated) with granulomatous nephritis and hypercalcemia
top5.rationale: South American exposure, calcified mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes, granulomatous renal infiltrate, and hypercalcemia from granulomatous inflammation fit endemic fungal infection.
In AIDS patients with CD4 <200 and negative standard STI workup, CMV is a leading cause of severe rectal pain/bleeding often missed without specific biopsy staining.
HIV-associated malignancy presenting as mass effect or ulceration causing pain/discharge; condylomas may obscure underlying neoplastic changes on external exam.
RPR can be falsely negative in early primary syphilis or due to prozone effect; rectal chancres are frequently misdiagnosed as hemorrhoids or fissures.
Causes severe proctocolitis with bloody/mucoid discharge and inguinal lymphadenopathy; routine NAATs for Chlamydia often miss LGV serovars unless specifically tested.
Family history is significant; HIV immunosuppression does not preclude IBD, and Crohn's can present with perianal disease and rectal bleeding mimicking infectious proctitis.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Nonseminomatous Germ Cell Tumor (Testicular Cancer)
top5.rationale: Unifies the triad of pulmonary 'cannonball' metastases, massive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and hepatic lesions in a young male; gynecomastia is explained by beta-hCG secretion causing hypogonadism (low LH/FSH) and direct estrogenic effects.

Can present with bulky thoracic disease and systemic symptoms (B-symptoms), but typically causes mediastinal/hilar adenopathy rather than the isolated lower-zone pulmonary nodules and retroperitoneal mass seen here; less likely to cause this specific pattern of gynecomastia.

Endemic fungal infection can mimic malignancy with pulmonary nodules, hepatosplenomegaly, and adrenal involvement (explaining fatigue/electrolyte issues), but the massive discrete liver masses and specific hormonal profile favor neoplasm.

Multisystem granulomatous disease affecting lungs, liver, and lymph nodes; however, sarcoidosis rarely presents with such large necrotic masses or significant gynecomastia, and the rapid weight loss/wasting is atypical for early-stage sarcoid.

top5.diagnosis: Combined Diagnosis: Graves' Disease and Metastatic Testicular Cancer
top5.rationale: The patient has confirmed hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, diffuse uptake on scintigraphy) which explains initial anxiety/tremors/fatigue, but this is an incidental comorbidity that does not explain the structural masses; the cancer is the primary driver of mortality risk.

The triad of a calcified testicular lesion, massive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and 'cannonball' pulmonary metastases in a young male is pathognomonic; gynecomastia results from beta-hCG secretion.

Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3 and diffuse uptake on scintigraphy confirms hyperthyroidism, likely an incidental autoimmune comorbidity given the negative thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic Hyperthyroidism due to hCG Cross-Reactivity
top5.rationale: While less likely than primary Graves' given the diffuse uptake pattern, high levels of tumor-derived hCG can stimulate the TSH receptor, mimicking or exacerbating thyrotoxicosis.
A specific subtype of NSGCT characterized by extremely high beta-hCG, which explains the severe gynecomastia, potential hemorrhagic metastases (hematochezia/anemia), and rapid clinical decline.

top5.diagnosis: Hepatic Metastasis with Secondary Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism
top5.rationale: Massive liver involvement and systemic illness suppress LH/FSH (as seen in labs), contributing to low-normal testosterone and worsening gynecomastia independent of hCG effects.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic germ cell tumor (non-seminomatous, likely mixed or yolk sac/choriocarcinoma component)
top5.rationale: Young male with right testicular calcification/mass, bulky retroperitoneal adenopathy, liver and lung metastases, gynecomastia (hCG), and fatigue/weight loss fits metastatic GCT despite normal AFP/hCG not shown.

top5.diagnosis: Primary mediastinal (or retroperitoneal) non-seminomatous germ cell tumor with extragonadal origin
top5.rationale: Extragonadal GCT can present with bulky retroperitoneal/pulmonary/liver masses and gynecomastia in a young male, even without a primary testicular lesion.

top5.diagnosis: Graves disease with incidental metastatic malignancy
top5.rationale: Diffuse thyroid uptake, suppressed TSH, elevated free T4, family history, and gynecomastia (from hyperthyroidism) explain thyroid findings but not the massive tumor burden.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell or Burkitt) with testicular involvement
top5.rationale: Young male with B symptoms, bulky retroperitoneal nodes, liver/lung masses, and testicular enlargement/calcification; can cause gynecomastia via hCG or hyperthyroidism-like state.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated infection (e.g., tuberculosis or endemic fungal) with immune-mediated thyroiditis and testicular involvement
top5.rationale: Subacute fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, pulmonary nodules, liver lesions, and retroperitoneal adenopathy could mimic malignancy; exposure history (tobacco chewing, travel not specified) and negative Lyme testing warrant consideration.

The triad of a young male with retroperitoneal adenopathy, pulmonary 'cannonball' metastases, and gynecomastia is pathognomonic; the small testicular calcification represents a burned-out primary tumor, while hCG secretion explains both the gynecomastia and the paraneoplastic hyperthyroidism.

While lymphadenopathy and masses fit, this diagnosis fails to explain the specific pattern of gynecomastia or the suppressed LH/FSH with normal testosterone, making it less likely than NSGCT despite being a common malignancy in this age group.

Can mimic malignancy with hepatosplenomegaly, lung nodules, and adrenal involvement (potentially explaining fatigue/hypotension), but does not account for the significant gynecomastia or the specific hormonal profile seen here.

top5.diagnosis: Concurrent Graves' Disease and Occult Malignancy
top5.rationale: This hypothesis attempts to separate the thyroid findings from the mass effect, but it ignores the unifying mechanism where high hCG levels cross-react with TSH receptors causing thyrotoxicosis, thus requiring two independent diagnoses instead of one.

A large abdominal mass with liver/lung mets could be ACC, potentially secreting estrogens to cause gynecomastia, but the presence of a distinct retroperitoneal nodal mass and the classic 'burned-out' testicular finding strongly favor germ cell origin over adrenal.

top5.diagnosis: Evans Syndrome (Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia and Immune Thrombocytopenia)
top5.rationale: The simultaneous presence of Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia and severe immune thrombocytopenia in an infant is the hallmark definition of Evans syndrome, which often presents with fever and rash as prodromal or associated inflammatory features.

Although rare in infants, SLE can present with hematologic abnormalities (AIHA, ITP) and cutaneous findings; the family history of splenomegaly and the severity of cytopenias warrant ruling out this unifying autoimmune etiology.

top5.diagnosis: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) or Primary Antibody Deficiency
top5.rationale: Primary immunodeficiencies frequently manifest with autoimmune cytopenias (Evans-like presentation) before recurrent infections become obvious; the low-normal IgG for age and specific lymphocyte subset patterns support an underlying immune dysregulation.

Malignancy must be excluded in any infant with pancytopenia/cytopenias, fever, and rash; while the smear lacks blasts, early marrow infiltration can present with peripheral cytopenias mimicking autoimmune disease.

This viral infection is a known trigger for both transient aplastic crisis and immune-mediated cytopenias (including Evans syndrome) in young children, potentially explaining the acute onset following a febrile illness.

top5.diagnosis: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) triggered by viral infection, with secondary autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Evans syndrome)
top5.rationale: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae/bruising in a well-appearing infant, positive direct antiglobulin test and falling hematocrit with reticulocytosis indicate combined immune-mediated platelet and red-cell destruction; the preceding urticaria and viral prodrome support an immune trigger.

top5.diagnosis: Parvovirus B19-associated pure red cell aplasia with immune thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: A viral infection can cause both severe thrombocytopenia and transient erythroblastopenia; the microcytic/hypochromic smear and reticulocyte response are atypical, but the combination of immune cytopenias and rash fits.

top5.diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by viral infection
top5.rationale: Fever, rash, cytopenias, elevated LDH, and a family history of splenomegaly could point to HLH; however, the absence of splenomegaly, hyperferritinemia, and hypofibrinogenemia makes this less likely.
Recent acetaminophen exposure could trigger immune-mediated platelet destruction; however, the positive DAT and anemia suggest a broader immune process, and acetaminophen is a rare cause.

A male infant with thrombocytopenia, eczema (urticaria), and immune dysregulation could have WAS; the normal platelet size and lack of severe immunodeficiency make this less likely, but it is a genetic cause of combined cytopenias.
Severe isolated thrombocytopenia followed by Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia and neutropenia defines Evans syndrome; the initial presentation mimics ITP.

The triad of cytopenias (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anemia), bone marrow failure signs (teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastic smear), and atypical lymphocytes is highly suspicious for malignancy despite normal blasts on peripheral smear.
Common viral trigger for transient aplastic crisis or immune-mediated cytopenias in infants; explains the preceding fever/rash and subsequent hematologic collapse.
Evans syndrome (autoimmune hemolytic anemia + ITP) can be the presenting feature of SLE in pediatric patients, supported by eosinophilia and potential renal involvement (creatinine fluctuation).
Rare genetic disorder causing severe thrombocytopenia in infancy that often progresses to pancytopenia and MDS/AML; must be ruled out given the age and severity.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical embolism through patent foramen ovale from pelvic/iliac vein thrombosis due to May–Thurner syndrome, with pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: Venous thrombus formed at the site of left common iliac vein compression, embolized to lungs and, via right-to-left PFO shunt, to the left MCA — explaining stroke, PE, elevated D-dimer, and troponin leak from right heart strain.

top5.diagnosis: Renal-cell carcinoma–associated hypercoagulable state (Trousseau syndrome) with venous thromboembolism and paradoxical embolic stroke
top5.rationale: The 7.5-cm necrotic renal mass provides an acquired prothrombotic stimulus; malignancy-driven hypercoagulability can produce venous thrombosis and, through PFO, arterial emboli — a cancer-associated thrombophilia that unifies all findings.

top5.diagnosis: May–Thurner syndrome (left common iliac vein compression) as the primary anatomic thrombogenic nidus
top5.rationale: Severe >50% stenosis of the left common iliac vein with collateral drainage is the structural lesion that seeded the iliofemoral thrombus responsible for both PE and paradoxical stroke; it is the overlooked anatomic companion finding.

top5.diagnosis: Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt as the conduit for paradoxical embolism
top5.rationale: Agitated-saline contrast echocardiography demonstrated right-to-left shunting, the necessary anatomic pathway allowing a venous thrombus to reach the left middle cerebral artery territory.

top5.diagnosis: Inherited or acquired thrombophilia (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome or factor V Leiden) superimposed on anatomic risk factors
top5.rationale: Though routine thrombophilia labs were normal, a young patient with unprovoked VTE, PE, and cryptogenic stroke warrants consideration of a coexisting hypercoagulable state; this could be overlooked if attention is fixed on the structural and malignant explanations.

top5.diagnosis: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) triggered by recent acetaminophen exposure
top5.rationale: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae/bruising in a well-appearing infant, no other cytopenias or coagulopathy; acetaminophen has been reported to trigger immune-mediated platelet destruction.
Infant with fever, rash, thrombocytopenia, and transient direct antiglobulin positivity; parvovirus is a classic cause of isolated thrombocytopenia and can be asymptomatic in household contacts.

top5.diagnosis: Human herpesvirus 6 (roseola infantum) with secondary ITP
top5.rationale: Age 6.5 months, fever and rash, no day care but two dogs and a cousin with splenomegaly; HHV-6 is a common infant infection that can cause transient thrombocytopenia and atypical lymphocytosis.

top5.diagnosis: Cow's milk protein–induced thrombocytopenia (food-protein–induced immune thrombocytopenia)
top5.rationale: Documented urticaria to milk-based formula, eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count up to 1560), and IgE 182 IU/ml suggest an allergic/immune diathesis that can rarely manifest as thrombocytopenia.

top5.diagnosis: Primary immunodeficiency (e.g., Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome or other combined immunodeficiency) presenting with ITP-like picture
top5.rationale: Male infant with thrombocytopenia, eczema/urticaria, and family history of splenomegaly; absence of day care and lack of sick contacts may reflect an underlying immune defect rather than simple exposure.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical embolism via patent foramen ovale from pelvic vein thrombosis due to May–Thurner syndrome, with pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: Transatlantic flight, chest pain/dyspnea before stroke, PFO with right-to-left shunt, bilateral PE, and left common iliac vein compression on pelvic MRA all support a venous thromboembolic source with paradoxical embolization.

top5.diagnosis: Renal-cell carcinoma with acquired hypercoagulable state (Trousseau syndrome) driving venous thromboembolism
top5.rationale: Incidental 7.5-cm enhancing necrotic right renal mass provides a prothrombotic stimulus that, combined with May–Thurner anatomy, explains unprovoked PE and cryptogenic stroke in a 49-year-old.

top5.diagnosis: May–Thurner syndrome (left common iliac vein compression) as the anatomic nidus for iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
top5.rationale: Pelvic MRA shows >50% left common iliac vein stenosis with collateral drainage; negative leg duplex does not exclude iliac vein thrombosis, and complete embolization may explain absent thrombus.

top5.diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism with elevated troponin and right-heart strain
top5.rationale: V/Q and CT angiography confirm multiple pulmonary artery filling defects; troponin elevation without coronary disease suggests right ventricular strain and increased mortality risk.

top5.diagnosis: Migraine with aura as a possible contributing stroke mechanism
top5.rationale: History of migraine headaches and recurrent left thigh swelling since childhood may reflect an underlying vascular/coagulable predisposition; migraine is a recognized, often overlooked risk factor for ischemic stroke in young women.

The triad of fever, rash, and cytopenias in an infant is a classic presentation for ALL; the 'normal' initial exam may miss subtle bone tenderness or lymphadenopathy, and the subsequent neutropenia/lymphocytosis pattern fits marrow infiltration.

Explains fever, cytopenias (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia), and potential liver/spleen involvement; the high ferritin (implied by inflammation) and hypertriglyceridemia are key missing data points that would confirm this life-threatening mimic of sepsis or leukemia.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) with Evans Syndrome
top5.rationale: The combination of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive DAT) and immune thrombocytopenia constitutes Evans syndrome, which can be the presenting feature of pediatric SLE, explaining the fever, rash, and multi-system lab abnormalities.

Can cause transient aplastic crisis (severe cytopenias) and erythrocyte membrane antibodies leading to positive DAT; the 'rash' may be misinterpreted fifth disease or vasculitic purpura, fitting the acute onset in an otherwise healthy child.

top5.diagnosis: Drug-Induced Immune Hemolytic Anemia and Thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: Recent acetaminophen use could trigger idiosyncratic drug-induced immune destruction of both RBCs and platelets, explaining the sudden onset, positive DAT, and rapid recovery after cessation/supportive care without underlying malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Sickle cell disease–related vasculopathy with acute ischemic stroke (large-vessel or branch atheromatous disease) involving the left posterior inferior frontal / parietal language network
top5.rationale: Underlying chronic hemolysis and endothelial injury from HbSS promote intimal hyperplasia and thrombosis; acute headache, aphasia, alexia/agraphia, and acalculia localize to dominant hemisphere, with multiple prior aneurysms reflecting fragile vasculature.

top5.diagnosis: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial aneurysm (sickle cell–associated aneurysm)
top5.rationale: Known multiple stable aneurysms plus acute severe headache and transient language/behavioral change could reflect sentinel bleed; however, lack of meningismus and relatively mild NIHSS make it less likely than ischemic event.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome (from bone marrow necrosis in sickle cell disease)
top5.rationale: Sickle cell vaso-occlusion can cause marrow necrosis and fat emboli, producing acute encephalopathy, headache, and focal deficits; petechiae and hypoxemia often absent, but J-point elevation and tachycardia could hint at systemic involvement.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (hypercoagulable state from sickle cell disease and marijuana use)
top5.rationale: Chronic hemolysis, dehydration, and cannabis use promote thrombosis; headache and language deficits can occur without fever or neck stiffness, though venous infarcts often have different imaging patterns.

top5.diagnosis: Primary central nervous system vasculitis (e.g., PACNS) or secondary vasculitis from sickle cell disease
top5.rationale: Recurrent headaches, multiple aneurysms, and acute stroke-like presentation in a young patient suggest inflammatory vasculopathy; histology would show transmural inflammation, and lab clues include elevated inflammatory markers (not yet reported).

top5.diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial aneurysm
top5.rationale: Known multiple intracranial aneurysms in a sickle cell patient with acute thunderclap headache, transient speech disturbance, and fluctuating deficits; sentinel bleed can present with mild NIHSS and no neck pain.

top5.diagnosis: Sickle cell disease–related ischemic stroke (large-vessel or small-vessel)
top5.rationale: Young African-American with sickle cell anemia, prior acute chest syndrome, and multiple aneurysms; acute aphasia, alexia, agraphia, and acalculia localize to dominant hemisphere and fit vaso-occlusive stroke.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome (from bone marrow necrosis in sickle cell crisis)
top5.rationale: Sickle cell patients can develop bone marrow necrosis with fat emboli causing headache, encephalopathy, and focal deficits; marijuana use and recent headache may mask a vaso-occlusive crisis.

Temporal onset after marijuana smoking in a young patient with headache and focal neurologic deficits; cannabis can trigger vasospasm or reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, especially in susceptible individuals.

top5.diagnosis: Infectious meningoencephalitis (e.g., HSV-1 or other viral) with sickle cell as risk factor
top5.rationale: Acute headache, confusion, aphasia, and feverless presentation can occur in viral encephalitis; sickle cell patients are functionally asplenic and at risk for encapsulated organisms, though lack of fever makes this less likely.

Mucopurulent rectal discharge, severe anorectal pain, blood in stools, and receptive anal intercourse in an HIV-positive man with preserved CD4 are classic for LGV serovars L1-L3; histology shows lymphoplasmacytic and granulomatous inflammation with possible crypt destruction, and NAAT of rectal swab is diagnostic.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) anorectal ulceration/proctitis
top5.rationale: Prior rectal herpes and ongoing high-risk receptive anal intercourse support HSV-2 reactivation; however, the negative rectal HSV swab and absence of visible ulcers make this less likely, though PCR from anoscopy-directed sampling may be needed.

History of disseminated MAC with CD4 count of 6 and incomplete immune reconstitution could produce granulomatous rectal inflammation; histology would show acid-fast bacilli and granulomas, but the relatively high CD4 count and lack of systemic symptoms make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Anal squamous cell carcinoma arising in condyloma acuminatum
top5.rationale: Bulky perianal condylomas, HIV, and smoking are risk factors; a malignancy could cause pain, bleeding, and discharge, and may be missed on anoscopy if proximal or infiltrative; biopsy would show invasive squamous cells with HPV-associated changes.

Receptive anal intercourse and mucopurulent discharge fit gonococcal proctitis, but the negative rectal swab culture and lack of response to ceftriaxone/azithromycin make this unlikely; however, culture sensitivity is imperfect and NAAT may be needed.

top5.diagnosis: Rectal lymphoma (non-Hodgkin's, AIDS-related, e.g., diffuse large B-cell or Burkitt)
top5.rationale: Despite immune reconstitution (CD4 188, VL <50), persistent rectal pain, bleeding, and mucus with negative cultures and condylomas point to a mass lesion; HIV-related lymphoma is a hidden risk in long-standing AIDS.
Bulky perianal condylomas (HPV-related) and receptive anal intercourse are strong risk factors; malignancy can present with pain, bleeding, and discharge despite negative HSV/gonorrhea testing.

top5.diagnosis: Proctitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis (lymphogranuloma venereum serovar)
top5.rationale: Mucopurulent rectal discharge, pain, and blood in an MSM with high-risk sexual exposures; routine swabs for gonorrhea and HSV were negative, but chlamydia testing was not reported.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus proctitis (acyclovir-resistant or atypical)
top5.rationale: History of rectal HSV and ongoing receptive anal intercourse; negative swab may reflect sampling error or resistance, and pain can be severe enough to preclude anoscopy.

top5.diagnosis: Methamphetamine-induced ischemic colitis or rectal ulceration
top5.rationale: Regular methamphetamine use can cause vasoconstriction and ischemic injury; this exposure is easily overlooked when focusing on infectious causes.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic germ cell tumor (nonseminomatous, likely mixed yolk sac/choriocarcinoma) of the right testis
top5.rationale: Young man with testicular calcification, asymmetric testis, massive retroperitoneal adenopathy, bulky hepatic and pulmonary metastases, gynecomastia (hCG-driven), and fatigue/weight loss — a single germ-cell clone explains all sites; hallmark: elevated AFP/hCG, i(12p), Schiller-Duval bodies or syncytiotrophoblasts.

top5.diagnosis: Primary mediastinal (or retroperitoneal) non-seminomatous germ cell tumor with hepatic and pulmonary spread
top5.rationale: Extragonadal germ cell tumor can present with bulky midline masses, gynecomastia from hCG, and a 'burned-out' testicular primary; molecular i(12p) and elevated AFP/hCG are the clinchers.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic choriocarcinoma with hyperthyroidism (tumor-derived hCG cross-reactivity with TSH receptor)
top5.rationale: The combination of suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, diffuse thyroid uptake, gynecomastia, and widespread hemorrhagic metastases is classic for hCG-secreting choriocarcinoma; histology shows biphasic trophoblast without villi.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell or Burkitt) with hepatic, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal involvement
top5.rationale: Can produce bulky nodal and extranodal masses, B symptoms, anemia, and elevated LDH; however, gynecomastia and testicular calcification are atypical, and thyroid stimulation is unexplained.

top5.diagnosis: Graves' disease as a paraneoplastic or coincident autoimmune phenomenon accompanying an occult malignancy
top5.rationale: Family history, diffuse thyroid uptake, and suppressed TSH fit Graves', but the striking systemic tumor burden and gynecomastia point to a paraneoplastic hCG effect rather than isolated autoimmune disease.
